c1e9467f7b.q: What are California's requirements for tracking driver hours when paying by the mile?
c1e9467f7b.a: California requires separate compensation for nonproductive time such as pre-trip inspections, waiting to load, and qualified rest periods. These hours cannot be counted in mileage-only pay; they must be tracked separately and paid according to applicable wage requirements. Simply paying a high mileage rate does not automatically satisfy these requirements—all work hours must be accounted for and paid correctly.

29987279b1.q: What is the difference between a customer's detention billing policy and a driver's work time for pay purposes?
29987279b1.a: A customer agreement stating detention billing begins after two hours is a billing arrangement only and does not determine whether the driver's first two hours count as paid work. Under California wage rules, drivers must be paid for all work time regardless of the customer's detention policy. Even if a shipper charges detention only after two hours, the driver must be paid for all time spent performing duties.

f: Complete driver work hour tracking improves business decisions beyond payroll compliance by enabling better conversations about pricing and scheduling. When fleets track all work time—not just driving miles—they can identify how identical loads have very different costs depending on factors like quick turnarounds versus extended waiting periods. This data reveals effective hourly earnings matter more than rate per mile alone, helping companies prioritize which customers to accept and understand why drivers complain about certain routes. The time records clarify the full picture of driver productivity and profitability that mileage alone cannot capture.

Additionally, accurate hour tracking supports better operational decisions through a structured review process. When operations personnel review time exceptions—such as confirming whether a driver actually waited five hours at a customer dock or was released to the truck stop—they provide payroll with verified information and help distinguish between different types of waiting that have different business implications. This collaborative process between operations and payroll creates a complete record of how time is spent, enabling management to make informed decisions about customer relationships, driver compensation structures, route planning, and operational efficiency based on actual work patterns rather than assumptions.

5a44fa981f.q: Why is dividing mileage earnings by total work hours insufficient to prove California wage compliance?
5a44fa981f.a: California requires separate compensation for specific categories of time, and dividing the total paycheck by hours does not prove that each required component has been paid separately. For example, calculating $28.68 per hour average from mileage earnings may look fair, but if nonproductive time and rest periods require their own separate calculations and wage statement entries, those must be tracked and paid distinctly—averaging does not satisfy the legal requirement.
